members.name: persuasion_a
members.instructions: In a chat where a persuader tries to get the partner to donate to Save the Children, tag the final 'Persuader message to tag' with the persuasion strategy or dialogue act it uses. Use the earlier chat only as context; judge the tagged message itself. Pick the single best tag.

criteria.greeting: Opening the conversation: hello, hi, how are you, nice to meet you, or answering the partner's how-are-you.
criteria.closing: Ending the conversation without thanking: goodbye, have a nice day, take care, nice talking to you.
criteria.thank: The persuader thanks the partner (for their time, donation, kindness or the chat), including a thank-you combined with a farewell.
criteria.acknowledgement: A short reply that acknowledges, agrees with or reacts positively to what the partner just said: yes, ok, I see, I agree, me too, I understand, great, wow, that's amazing, glad to hear it.
criteria.praise-user: Credits the partner personally: says they are kind, generous, caring or a good person, or praises their generosity in deciding to give. A generic positive reaction that does not credit the partner is acknowledgement.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks whether the partner is aware of or familiar with Save the Children, or what they know about it.
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks the partner's opinion, experience or habits about donating, charities or the cause (do you give to charities, what do you think about this, are you interested, any questions).
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the partner's personal life unrelated to donating: family, children, where they live, work, hobbies, weather, their day.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Directly asks or urges the partner to donate (would you like to donate, will you give some of your payment, please donate), without asking for a specific amount.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks how much the partner will or would like to donate.
criteria.donation-information: Explains how donating works: the donation comes out of the task payment, the research team sends it to the charity, the amount is entirely up to the partner (anything between nothing and their whole payment, whatever they are comfortable with), when and where to enter it, other ways to pay; also explaining what this chat is for (that they are here to discuss donating to the charity).
criteria.credibility-appeal: Builds the charity's credibility with facts about the organisation: what Save the Children is and does, where it works, its programs, history, size, reputation, ratings, how much of the money reaches programs, its website, the persuader speaking as a member of Save the Children about their own job in it, concrete current arrangements such as matching partnerships (even when the message ends by saying any amount helps); also arguments that it can be trusted because of its age, scale or reputation.
criteria.logical-appeal: Reasons that giving makes sense: the donation will make a concrete difference, the money helps children, any donation helps, the charity relies on donations, children are the future, everyone giving a little adds up, the partner's own stated values imply giving.
criteria.emotion-appeal: Tries to evoke feelings: facts or statistics about children's suffering, death, hunger or danger, describing their plight, asking the partner to imagine it, saying how sad or heartbreaking it is, or how good helping feels; reminding the partner of their own child or family so they picture the children's plight; also contrasting the comfortable life the persuader or partner has had with what these children lack, to stir gratitude or guilt.
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Uses the smallness of the amount to make giving easy: even the smallest or tiniest donation makes a difference, it only takes pocket change, you can give as little as a few cents, such an amount is nothing to people like us, could you spare just a tiny amount. Arguing that many small gifts add up to a large total across donors is logical-appeal. A general claim that any donation helps, without stressing how small it can be, is logical-appeal.
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader states their own donation to Save the Children or to this drive, their intention to donate, or their habit of giving to this charity, as a model for the partner (they will donate too, will match the partner's donation, they give to this charity regularly), including when answering the partner's question about it.
criteria.personal-story: Narrates a specific event or experience: something that happened to the persuader (a trip, work abroad, something they saw), or what happened to a particular person or child; also the persuader sharing their own hardships or struggles to relate to the partner's difficulties.
criteria.persuader-small-talk: The persuader shares facts about their own life while chatting or answering the partner's personal questions: where they live, their plans, their job or volunteer work for other employers or causes, or their giving to causes in general that is not tied to Save the Children or this donation. Excludes the persuader speaking as a member of Save the Children itself about their job there (credibility-appeal), narrated trips or experiences (personal-story), hardships shared to relate (personal-story), and remarks contrasting their comfortable upbringing with the children's needs (emotion-appeal).
criteria.off-task: Talk about something unrelated to the charity, the donation and either person's life: correcting a typo, unrelated topics such as history or politics.
criteria.chat-logistics: Remarks about the chat itself: how many turns are left, what the study requires, that the conversation must continue.
criteria.confirm-donation: Checks or confirms the partner's decision: repeats the amount they chose, or asks whether they really mean to give nothing.
criteria.you-are-welcome: Responds to the partner's thanks: you're welcome, no problem.
criteria.other: Anything else: unclear fragments, non-English, persuader's opinions or answers that fit none of the above.
